title: Behaviour tests for splitEvenly
prompt:
The subject's comment lists `splitEvenly`'s contract. Write tests for that contract (not for how the function is written) until your suite passes on the real code and catches four hidden bugs:

- one drops the leftover cents,
- one hands out one leftover cent too many,
- one gives the leftover cents to the **last** people instead of the first,
- one returns an empty array for zero people instead of throwing.

A `sum` helper is already in the starter.
hints: Inputs that divide evenly (like 900 between 3) hide every remainder bug. Use totals that leave a remainder, such as 1000 between 3 or 1001 between 4.
The sum invariant catches two of the bugs at once: `expect(sum(splitEvenly(1000, 3))).toBe(1000)`.
For the order rule, compare the whole array: `splitEvenly(1001, 4)` must equal `[251, 250, 250, 250]`. For zero people, use `expect(() => splitEvenly(1000, 0)).toThrow(RangeError)`.
explanation: The sum invariant does the heavy lifting: dropping the remainder makes the total too small and the off-by-one makes it too big, so one assertion kills both. The order rule is part of the documented contract, so asserting the exact array is a behaviour test, not an implementation test; it is the only way to catch the version that favours the last people, which still conserves money and stays fair. The zero-people case is a boundary that silently returned `[]` in the buggy version, and a caller would have divided a bill between nobody. None of these tests mention `Math.floor`, `%` or `Array.from`, so you can rewrite the function freely and they stay green.

checks.passes: All your tests pass against the real splitEvenly
checks.catches-drops-remainder: Catches the version that drops leftover cents
checks.catches-extra-cent: Catches the version that hands out one cent too many
checks.catches-remainder-last: Catches the version that gives leftover cents to the last people
checks.catches-zero-people: Catches the version that accepts zero people
